full_text_en:
Marinaviva Copanaviera v. China National Metals and Minerals Import and Export Corporation

Demurrage Dispute

Plaintiff: Marinaviva Copanaviera (MARINAVIVACOPANIANAVIERA).

Defendant: China National Metals and Minerals Import and Export Corporation.

In the case of demurrage dispute between the plaintiff, Marinaviva Copanaviera, and the defendant, China National Metals and Minerals Import and Export Corporation, the plaintiff applied to the Qingdao Maritime Court for an order to detain the defendant's cargo on board the vessel "KEFALONIA HOPE" as security for the accrued demurrage (USD 395,600) and continuing demurrage.

After accepting the case, the Qingdao Maritime Court found the following facts: On October 9, 1984, the defendant (hereinafter referred to as the Buyer) entered into a sales contract with Hugo New & Sons International Sales Corp., New York, USA (hereinafter referred to as the Seller). The contract provided that the Buyer would import 24,000 metric tons of scrap iron and steel from the United States on a cost and freight (C&F) basis; the Seller would arrange the vessel, loading from a port on the East Coast of the United States, with a shipping period from October 20 to November 30, 1984, and the discharge port was Dalian, China. Clause 6(1) of the additional terms of the contract stipulated: "At the discharge port, cargo shall be discharged at the rate of 1,500 metric tons per weather working day of 24 consecutive hours (holidays excluded). Demurrage shall be USD 4,500 per day, and demurrage time shall run continuously."

On November 9, 1984, the Seller entered into a charter party with the Panamanian company Marinaviva Copanaviera, chartering the vessel "KEFALONIA HOPE" owned by the latter. The charter party stipulated that demurrage would be calculated at USD 4,600 per day; the shipowner was entitled to a lien.

After loading the Buyer's cargo of 24,755.5 metric tons at the ports of Providence, Rhode Island, and Boston, Massachusetts, USA, the "KEFALONIA HOPE" issued order bills of lading on November 29 and December 6, 1984, respectively, with China National Foreign Trade Transportation Corporation as the notify party. The vessel departed from Boston on December 7, 1984, and arrived at the discharge port of Dalian on January 18, 1985. Upon arrival, the vessel tendered a Notice of Readiness and anchored at the anchorage awaiting discharge, but the port did not commence discharge. Subsequently, Dalian Ocean Shipping Agency notified the vessel to move to Qingdao for discharge. The vessel arrived at Qingdao on February 13 and did not start discharge until March 14. On May 9, 1985, the shipowner applied to the Qingdao Maritime Court to detain the cargo remaining on board belonging to the consignee and requested that the consignee immediately pay the accrued demurrage of USD 395,600 and the demurrage that might continue to accrue until discharge was completed. The basis was Clause 8 of the charter party, which provided: "The shipowner shall have a lien on the cargo for freight, deadfreight, and demurrage," and the bills of lading issued by the master contained an "incorporation clause" stating "all other conditions and exceptions as per charter party," making the demurrage clause in the charter party equally binding on the consignee, and "to ensure the shipowner collects all demurrage, the shipowner is entitled to lien the cargo."

Upon review, the Qingdao Maritime Court held that the lien on cargo claimed by the plaintiff arose from the vessel's demurrage, and the charter party contained a lien clause. Although the defendant was not a party to the charter party, the document held by the defendant for taking delivery of the cargo was a bill of lading issued under the charter party, which contained an "incorporation clause" stating "all other conditions and exceptions as per charter party." Therefore, the demurrage clause in the charter party was binding on the holder of the bill of lading, i.e., the defendant in this case, and the defendant should pay the demurrage to the plaintiff. The plaintiff's application to detain the cargo on board to secure its claim was justified.

Accordingly, on May 10, 1985, the Qingdao Maritime Court ruled: "The plaintiff's application to detain the defendant's cargo is granted. Delivery of the cargo shall cease from the time this ruling is served. The defendant is ordered to provide a letter of credit guarantee from the Bank of China to the Qingdao Maritime Court within five days. Unless the plaintiff and the defendant reach a settlement, this Court will exercise its jurisdiction over this case."

On May 14, the defendant provided a letter of credit guarantee through the Bank of China and requested the continuation of cargo delivery. On the same day, the Qingdao Maritime Court lawfully ruled to accept the letter of credit guarantee from the Bank of China provided by the defendant and ordered the plaintiff to continue delivery of the detained cargo from the time this ruling was served.

On May 28, 1985, the plaintiff and the defendant negotiated on the specific amount of demurrage and the method of payment and reached the following settlement agreement:

1. The plaintiff agreed to grant a special deduction of 9.5% from the demurrage of USD 498,901.92 for 108.5 days;
2. The defendant would pay the plaintiff the demurrage after the deduction, totaling USD 451,506.24.

Thereupon, the plaintiff applied to have the Bank of China's guarantee released from its binding effect on the defendant. On July 25, 1985, the Qingdao Maritime Court reviewed the matter and held that the agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant was reached on the basis of the court's clarification of the facts and apportionment of liability, was consistent with the provisions of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation) and international customary practice, and could be permitted. Therefore, the court ruled to release the Bank of China's guarantee from its binding effect on the defendant, China National Metals and Minerals Import and Export Corporation.

At its 246th session on March 3, 1986, the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, in accordance with Article 11, Paragraph 1 of the Organic Law of the People's Courts of the People's Republic of China, concluded in summarizing trial experience that, in handling this case, the Qingdao Maritime Court had impartially administered justice in accordance with the law, safeguarding the dignity of state law and the lawful rights and interests of the parties, and that this case could serve as a reference for people's courts nationwide.
